blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en:
Recent years have witnessed the rapid adoption of reinforcement learning (RL)
in large language model (LLM) post-training, with substantial gains in
mathematical reasoning and code generation. In practical systems, however,
policy updates and differences between rollout and training engines can make
sampled responses off-policy. Sequence-level masking addresses this
mismatch by deciding whether an entire response should contribute to
optimization. A common masking rule uses the length-normalized geometric mean
of sampled token probability ratios. Its signed log-ratios can cancel across
positions, concealing substantial bidirectional policy drift. We propose Cancellation-Aware Response Masking (CARM), a sequence-level mask
that takes the absolute value of each token log-ratio before averaging,
preventing opposing probability changes from canceling. We prove that
accepted responses satisfy a joint bound on the fraction of sampled-token
ratios outside a prescribed band and their mean log-distance beyond its
boundaries. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation
show that CARM improves mean@16
averaged over AIME 2024/2025/2026 and BeyondAIME by up to 3.13 3.13 percentage
points over geometric-mean masking, and increases average pass@1 across four
code benchmarks by 2.88 2.88 points over the strongest evaluated baseline.
These findings support CARM as a theoretically grounded and effective
method for response-level off-policy control in LLM reinforcement learning.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Reinforcement learning (RL) is widely used to improve the reasoning ability of
large language models (LLMs), building on advances in preference-based
alignment and execution-feedback learning ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Le et al., 2022 ) .
In an ideal on-policy setting, responses are generated by the same policy
that is being optimized. In practical systems, however, several effects
introduce policy mismatch. Mini-batch optimization makes stored responses
stale as the policy changes, while actor–learner latency can delay their
use. High-throughput rollout engines may also differ from the training
backend in batching, numerical precision, and kernel implementations ( Yao et al., 2025 ; Sheng et al., 2025 ) . Consequently, the policy being
updated can assign substantially different probabilities to sampled tokens
than the rollout policy that generated them.

blocks.en:
Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) and Group Relative Policy Optimization
(GRPO) regulate policy updates through clipping in their token-level
surrogate losses ( Schulman et al., 2017 ; Shao et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) .
Clipping changes how individual tokens contribute to the loss, but does not
keep every current-to-rollout probability ratio within a prescribed interval.
It also does not decide whether an entire response should participate in
the update. Sequence-level masking complements clipping by making this
decision from a score that summarizes mismatch across the response.
Trust Region Masking (TRM), for example, motivates such filtering through
an analysis of how policy mismatch affects optimization over long
autoregressive sequences ( Li et al., 2026 ) .

blocks.en:
A simple response-level criterion is geometric-mean masking: it takes the
geometric mean of the token probability ratios and retains responses when
this aggregate is close to one. We refer to this baseline as GeoMean .
In log space, this aggregation corresponds to averaging signed token
log-ratios, as used in DeepSeek-V3.2’s off-policy sequence mask ( Liu et al., 2025a ) . The problem is that positive and negative
log-ratios can cancel. For example, token ratios of 10 10 and 0.1 0.1 have a
geometric mean of one, although each sampled-token probability has changed
tenfold. More generally, a response can appear well aligned under this
score because its probability changes balance out, rather than because
those changes are small.

magnitudes. CARM changes which responses contribute to optimization

blocks.en:
Beyond preventing cancellation, CARM gives the response-level
threshold a direct token-level interpretation. We prove that every accepted
response satisfies a joint bound on the fraction of sampled-token ratios
outside a prescribed, possibly asymmetric band and their mean log-distance
beyond its boundaries. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code
generation show improvements over token- and sequence-level baselines.
Threshold analyses further show that similar filtering rates can yield
different accuracies, while filtering more responses is not consistently
better.

blocks.en:
Our contributions are: • We formalize cancellation in signed-log sequence masking: the
aggregate score can indicate perfect apparent alignment even when every
sampled token ratio violates a prescribed band. • We propose CARM, a sequence-level mask that prevents cancellation
by taking absolute values before averaging token log-ratios. We derive a
joint bound on the frequency and severity of ratio-band violations in
accepted responses, including asymmetric bands, giving the filtering
threshold a token-level interpretation. • Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation show
improvements over sequence- and token-level baselines. Paired-response
diagnostics and threshold analyses characterize the selection behavior:
higher accuracy is observed at comparable average filtering rates, and
accuracy is not monotone in the masked fraction.

blocks.en: 2 Related Work
blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en:
Policy optimization for LLM post-training. Trust Region Policy Optimization (TRPO) constrains Kullback–Leibler (KL)
divergence, while PPO uses a clipped-ratio surrogate ( Schulman et al., 2015 ; Schulman et al., 2017 ) . GRPO replaces a learned critic with
within-group relative advantages ( Shao et al., 2024 ) .
Answer correctness and program execution provide reward signals for improving
mathematical reasoning and code generation ( Le et al., 2022 ; Dou et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2025 ; Zeng et al., 2026 ) ,
complementing inference-time reasoning and program-aided prompting ( Wei et al., 2022 ; Chen et al., 2023 ; Gao et al., 2023 ) .
Decoupled Clip and Dynamic sAmpling Policy Optimization (DAPO) refines
clipping and sampling ( Yu et al., 2025 ) ; related work revisits advantage
normalization, sequence-level objectives, and reward–policy learning ( Hu et al., 2025 ; Xie et al., 2025 ; Lu et al., 2026a ) .
These choices determine how sampled responses contribute to optimization.
CARM addresses the complementary question of whether a sampled response
should contribute to the current policy update.

blocks.en:
Off-policy and token-level trust-region control. This selection problem arises even in nominally online training: actor–learner
delay, repeated updates, and rollout–training engine differences separate
the policy that generates responses from the policy being optimized ( Espeholt et al., 2018 ; Yao et al., 2025 ; Sheng et al., 2025 ) .
Importance weighting and token-level filtering control individual update
contributions ( Espeholt et al., 2018 ; Shen et al., 2025 ) . Adaptive clipping
balances advantage contributions and mitigates entropy loss ( Xi et al., 2026 ) , while divergence-based controls constrain update size ( Qi et al., 2026 ; Yao et al., 2026 ) . These mechanisms regulate the update within a
response. CARM instead decides whether to retain the complete response,
separating response selection from the surrogate applied to retained tokens.

blocks.en:
Sequence-level correction and masking. Response-level selection must summarize mismatch across an entire sampled
path. Length-normalized geometric aggregation removes the direct length
dependence of multiplying token ratios ( Liu et al., 2025b ) ; it also
underlies sequence-level clipping in Group Sequence Policy Optimization
(GSPO) ( Zheng et al., 2025a ) .
DeepSeek-V3.2 explicitly uses off-policy sequence masking based on the mean
signed log-ratio, equivalently the logarithm of a length-normalized
geometric-mean ratio, to stabilize GRPO training ( Liu et al., 2025a ) .
Its rule applies a one-sided threshold to negative-advantage responses.
Our GeoMean baseline uses
the same signed-log aggregation with reciprocal-band acceptance
(Eq. 5 ); we examine advantage conditioning separately
in Section 5.2 .
TRM takes a
worst-position view, rejecting a response when its maximum token-level
divergence violates a long-horizon trust region ( Li et al., 2026 ) .
CARM targets a different limitation: geometric aggregation averages
signed log-ratios, so opposing shifts can cancel. Averaging their absolute
values measures bidirectional drift rather than net displacement. The
resulting mask changes which responses contribute to the update while
retaining the token-level policy surrogate.

blocks.en: 6 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 6 结论

blocks.en:
We proposed CARM, a response-level off-policy mask that
averages absolute token log-ratios to
prevent opposing probability changes from canceling. Our analysis shows that signed aggregation
can accept responses even when every sampled-token ratio lies outside a reciprocal-symmetric band.
In contrast, CARMbounds the frequency and severity of ratio-band violations through a joint budget
for each accepted response, giving the threshold a token-level interpretation. Experiments show
gains in mathematical reasoning and code generation over the evaluated baselines, together with improved sampling consistency.
These findings support CARM as a principled response-selection
criterion that complements reward-directed PPO/GRPO optimization.

blocks.en:
We store the sampled-token log-probabilities produced during rollout.
During training, each optimizer mini-batch is divided into micro-batches;
each micro-batch forward supplies the current log-probabilities used by both
the response mask and the token surrogate. The optimizer updates the policy
after gradient accumulation over the mini-batch. Threshold comparisons
produce a binary gate with no gradient through the decision, as represented
by stopgrad \operatorname{stopgrad} in Algorithm 1 .
Masking is local to loss evaluation rather than permanent removal from the rollout batch.
Our experiments use one optimization epoch per rollout batch;
with multiple epochs, the gate would be recomputed whenever a response is evaluated under the updated policy.
